Press Release:


Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 – Five Years On
It was a routine scheduled flight from Kuala Lumpur International Airport to Beijing Capital International Airport, carrying 239 passengers and crew – but five years ago Malaysian Airlines flight MH370 disappeared from the radar while flying over the Indian Ocean. An intensive search and investigation followed with some of the world’s top investigators, but with little progress over the years, it remains unclear why the plane went down. Now for the first time investigators have opened up the vault which contains the only recovered parts of the wreckage from the doomed flight.
Producer: ABC Australia


Script:


YSIX 2019005 01 60 MINUTES 03MAR2019
MH370: NEVER GIVE UP**

PARTS 1, 2, 3

For her first assignment on 60 MINUTES, Sarah Abo investigates new developments in the mystery of Malaysia Airlines flight MH370. It's now five years since it disappeared, but there have been no definitive answers about where the airliner is or what happened to it. The failure of the search has had an unbearable impact on the family and friends of the 239 people on board, who are presumed dead. But Danica Weeks, whose husband Paul was one of the passengers, refuses to give up. With Sarah Abo's assistance, she has achieved what many think is impossible and arranged a face-to-face meeting with the Malaysian Prime Minister, Dr Mahathir bin Mohamad – the first time he has met with a relative of a passenger on MH370. The Perth mother-of-two has pleaded with him to continue searching for the plane. And as our story reveals, Dr Mahathir has been clearly touched by Danica Weeks' determination, ordering his Minister of Transport to give 60 MINUTES world-first access to the secret vault where recovered parts of the plane's wreckage are stored. It's a degree of investigative transparency from Malaysia that is unheard of, and signals a major step forward. Danica says it is vital that the world finds out what happened to MH370. "This is not just about the 239 people on the Boeing 777, this is about eight million people who get on a flight every day," she says.

Reporter: Sarah Abo
Producer: Gareth Harvey
Crew: Richard Malone, Micky Breen
Editor: Andrew Page
SM: 11/19
Duration: Part 1: 10:03 / Part 2: 6:34 / Part 3: 9:53

**FOOTAGE CANNOT BE USED WITHOUT PERMISSION FROM THE SUPERVISING PRODUCER - 60 MINUTES**

KEYWORDS: evidence, Kuala Lumpur court buildings, Kuala Lumpur markets and shops, Kuala Lumpur traffic, Malaysia Airlines plane, Malaysian Prime Minister's residence, MH370 wreckage part, planes landing,political rally, Qantas plane, right outboard flap,

PART 1

SARAH ABO:
Good evening and welcome to 60 Minutes. I'm Sarah Abo. It's not just the despairing family and friends of the 239 men, women and children who were on board Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 who deserve answers about what happened to the plane. Everyone who flies needs to know where the Boeing 777 is, and why it ended up there. Big, modern airliners just can't vanish without explanation. In a few days, there'll be another grim MH370 milestone – it'll be five years since the plane went missing. But Danica Weeks, whose husband Paul was a passenger, will never lose hope this mystery will eventually be solved. And to help, she's meeting Malaysia's prime minister, Dr Mahathir Mohamad, to convince him more must be done.

(MUSIC)

SPEAKER:
You have to go through here. And into the middle.

DANICA WEEKS:
Into the middle. Oh, this is the real maze. Maze of all mazes.

SARAH ABO:
The enduring pain of MH370 is written in lives like Danica Weeks and her sons, eight-year-old Lincoln and six-year-old Jack. How does a mother tell them their father Paul is never coming back? That no-one even knows where he is.

DANICA WEEKS:
You know, when you look at Lincoln and Jack, I mean, look at them. They're six and eight. I mean, they were babies. And I just go, "What happened?" It just… It tears at you because you know what Pauly wanted to do with them, and he's not there, and I don't even know where the hell he is. And I just feel so awful. I just want to bring him back. I just want to grab him.

(MUSIC)

SARAH ABO:
MH370. It's the flight number that will haunt public imagination.

SPEAKER:
The Boeing 777 is missing. Flight MH370 would vanish from radar contact.

SARAH ABO:
The early hours of March 8, 2014. 239 men, women and children perished. No clue to their fate has ever been found.

DANICA WEEKS:
Every single plane crash has an answer. MH370, we have nothing.

SARAH ABO:
But could things be about to change, with Malaysia's strongman prime minister back in charge. Mr Prime Minister, what do you think happened to MH370? Tonight, an unprecedented meeting with Dr Mahathir and, on his order, access to the investigation's secret vault. Is this flap the smoking gun of aviation's greatest mystery?

(MUSIC INTENSIFIES)

SPEAKER:
If you look very carefully, really carefully, you can see it's actually a turn to the left. Then start a long turn to the right and then do another left turn.

SARAH ABO:
In the five years since MH370 disappeared, 60 Minutes has been chasing the truth.

SPEAKER (JOHN):
Every day that went by, the mystery grew deeper and this became very quickly unlike any accident in aviation's history.

SARAH ABO:
With every new breakthrough, suspicion – even certainty to some aviation experts – has closed in on MH370's captain Zaharie Ahmad Shah.

SPEAKER:
He was killing himself. Unfortunately, he was killing everybody else on board and he did it deliberately.

SARAH ABO:
But in all that time, those in charge of the Malaysian investigation have never agreed to answer the allegation that the pilot in command committed the worst crime in aviation history.

SPEAKER:
That's it.

SARAH ABO:
Until now.

(MUSIC)

FUAD SHARUJI:
I went numb. That is one of the airline's nightmare. It's my nightmare that, to find out that one of our flights have gone missing.

SARAH ABO:
Crisis manager Fuad Sharuji was in charge of Malaysia Airlines' response on that terrible day five years ago. He's one of the top-level players in the MH370 tragedy who's now speaking for the first time. How many things went wrong that night?

FUAD SHARUJI:
Everything went wrong.

SARAH ABO:
In all your decades of experience, has anything like this ever happened before?

FUAD SHARUJI:
No, never.

(MUSIC)

FUAD SHARUJI:
It was on the early morning of March 8 at 2:30 in the morning when I received the first phone call that we have lost contact with MH370. And I knew that there was something wrong, seriously wrong. So, we immediately activated our code red. I left my house immediately to our emergency operation centre.

SARAH ABO:
Fuad was not only managing a crisis unlike any in aviation history. For him, it was also personal. The man at the controls of MH370 was a man he knew well - popular Malaysia Airlines pilot Captain Zaharie Ahmad Shah.

SARAH ABO:
Was there anything peculiar about his final words?

FUAD SHARUJI:
His final words was, "Goodnight, MH370."

RADIO TRANSMISSION:
Goodnight, Malaysia 370.

FUAD SHARUJI:
His voice was calm, relatively calm. There was no signs of anxiety at all. There was nothing abnormal with his last words.

EAN HIGGINS:
Most people in the professional aviation industry believe that after that transmission, Zaharie hijacked his own aircraft, killed those on board by depressurising it and flew it to its doom in the middle of nowhere in the Southern Indian Ocean.

SARAH ABO:
For journalist and author Ean Higgins, MH370 has become a professional obsession. What would the world have been thinking when MH370 went missing?

EAN HIGGINS:
Well, I think the world would have been thinking that this plane must be found and will be found within a few days. Because they are always found, the wreckage, or whatever, or the debris. And people thought, well, one, two, three, four days, we'll have the answer to the mystery.

SARAH ABO:
In Perth, Danica Weeks and her then infant sons at home were waiting for a call from her husband, Paul, due to land in Beijing on MH370. Two weeks later, Charles Wooley was with her when Malaysia Airlines finally declared there was no hope.

SPEAKER:
This news was very devastating for the families.

DANICA WEEKS:
I remember saying then that 18 days was such a long time to wait. 1,800 days has been hell on earth.

SARAH ABO:
For the last five years, Danica has refused to give up hope of finding an answer for what happened to Paul. Now that hope is taking her to Malaysia. For weeks, on Danica's behalf, 60 Minutes has been in contact with Malaysia's iconic leader, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohammed. And in a move that stunned even his closest advisors, he has agreed for the first time to meet a relative of one of those lost on MH370. Danica will plead her case directly to Dr Mahathir. To reopen the investigation, to renew the search for the flight that took her husband.

DANICA WEEKS:
We're here for a very good reason, darling. To help find Daddy.

SARAH ABO:
Do you see this meeting with Dr Mahathir as your last hope?

DANICA WEEKS:
Yes. This is it. This is my last ditch effort. And as I say, is the pinnacle, it's as high as I can go. It'd just be nice to speak with him and really get him to understand where us, as the families, are coming from.

SARAH ABO:
How significant is it in your view that Dr Mahathir has agreed to meet with Danica?

EAN HIGGINS:
I think it's very significant. I think what it shows is that, despite all, he is open to listening to the possibility of re-opening a search. And, of course, if he were to decide on such a course of action, the country, which supports him greatly, would be right behind him.

(MUSIC)

SARAH ABO:
What makes this meeting remarkable is that for years, authorities here have closed ranks against foreigners scrutinising Malaysia's handling of MH370, defending the country's reputation with official silence. But with Dr Mahathir's new government, that silence may be breaking. Coming up, damning evidence. The smoking gun is an eerie course he plotted on a home flight simulator program. Why MH370's captain is to blame.

SPEAKER:
There is nowhere to land anywhere even close to that part of the world.

SARAH ABO:
And why Malaysia says he isn't.

PETER CHONG:
Commit mass murder, no way.

SARAH ABO:
No possibility?

PETER CHONG:
No possibility. Certainly not the Captain Zaharie that I know.


PART 2

SARAH ABO:
Five years on and the theories about what happened to MH370 range from the mystifying to the ridiculous. But the one that most international experts now believe is the only reasonable explanation based on known facts is that MH370 was hijacked by its own pilot, Zaharie Ahmad Shah, who then committed an act of mass murder. But while his name rings in infamy around the world, here in Malaysia, his innocence is an almost sacred truth.

EAN HIGGINS:
I think it's pretty simple. They don't want to lose face. It's very important in Asian cultures. It's a government owned airline and it's not a good look for Malaysia to have one of its nationals, one of its pilots, take 238 innocent people to their deaths.

SARAH ABO:
But Malaysia Airlines' crisis manager Fuad Sharuji will always defend his captain. For the record, did Captain Zaharie deliberately crash MH370 into the Southern Indian Ocean and kill everyone on board?

FUAD SHARUJI:
We don't believe so. For a person to actually take the lives of 239 passengers and crew on board, including his own life, must be a completely deranged person. Madman, crazy. And none of that is the character of Captain Zaharie.

PETER CHONG:
Anybody that knows Captain would immediately tell you that he's not this kind of person that would do such a thing.

SARAH ABO:
Peter Chong is another close friend of Zaharie Ahmad Shah. The two were bonded by their passion for politics, which some speculate was the motivation for Captain Zaharie to deliberately crash his plane.

So he was very politically active?

PETER CHONG:
He was very politically concerned.

SARAH ABO:
Have you allowed yourself to believe that Captain Zaharie did commit mass murder?

PETER CHONG:
To commit mass murder, no way.

SARAH ABO:
No possibility?

PETER CHONG:
No possibility. Certainly not the Captain Zaharie that I know.

SARAH ABO:
Do you accept that you may not have really known him? I mean, do we really know people?

PETER CHONG:
Obviously, there is a possibility, but very small percentage.

SARAH ABO:
Once of the greatest mysteries in the riddle of MH370 is how and where Captain Zaharie spent his final days and hours. Was this a man preparing to commit one aviation's most terrible and heartless crimes? And if so, why? Captain Zaharie's last hours alive could provide the telling clue.

SARAH ABO:
Those who point to Zaharie's guilt believe he was outraged at the trumped-up conviction of a man he believed was Malaysia's political saviour – Anwar Ibrahim. The conviction was handed down just hours before Captain Zaharie took off in MH370. There's also speculation he left a note behind, never revealed by the authorities. Journalist Ean Higgins.

EAN HIGGINS:
It was a pretty extraordinary coincidence. But did he leave a message and either it was never found or it got into other hands? Unless there's some part of the puzzle we don't know about, is that there was no claim of responsibility. What's the point of doing something like that, making a political protest, if you don't let anyone know why you're doing it?

SARAH ABO:
While a motive for Captain Zaharie's involvement is almost impossible to pinpoint, to many, the smoking gun of his guilt is an eerie course he plotted on his home flight simulator program only weeks before he guided MH370 into the night skies of Kuala Lumpur. The course mapped by Captain Zaharie is chillingly close to the presumed actual route of MH370.

EAN HIGGINS:
It made no sense whatsoever. It went up the Straits of Malacca, as MH370 did, and turned left, south, to the Southern Indian Ocean. There's nowhere to land anywhere even close to that part of the world. It could only have been a suicide flight.

SARAH ABO:
But despite this damning evidence, senior Malaysian officials still maintain there was nothing suspicious about Captain Zaharie's flight simulation. Even though, for the first time tonight, they admit it did stand out amongst the thousand other flight simulations recovered from his computer.

FUAD SHARUJI:
It's nothing unusual for pilots to have simulators at home, and to use that for training.

SARAH ABO:
Why do you think he would've tracked a course deep into the Southern Indian Ocean?

FUAD SHARUJI:
OK. He also tracked 1,000 other flights.

SARAH ABO:
Mm-hm. Did any of them end in the middle of nowhere?

FUAD SHARUJI:
Only one out of the 1,000 flights was in the South Indian Ocean.

SARAH ABO:
To land nowhere. Does that make sense?

FUAD SHARUJI:
I do not know. I cannot explain to you why that one particular flight landed in the South Indian Ocean. But if you are trying to lead me that he tried to ditch aircraft, I wouldn't want to buy that.

SARAH ABO:
Why would you map a route to the middle of nowhere?

PETER CHONG:
Because it's a difficult route. For training purposes, that would be ideal.

SARAH ABO:
But I don't understand. It's a difficult route to where? Where is he hoping to land the plane?

PETER CHONG:
In the water somewhere, maybe.

SARAH ABO:
He's intending to land the plane in the water?

PETER CHONG:
No. For training purposes.

SARAH ABO:
So, is it a coincidence that it did happen?

PETER CHONG:
Never know. History may tell us.

SARAH ABO:
Coming up, inside the investigation's secret vault. It is eerie to think this fragment represents a giant aircraft lying somewhere at the bottom of an ocean with its passengers and crew. A desperate plea to Malaysia's leader…

DANICA WEEKS:
Please don't give up on us.

SARAH ABO:
..and fresh hope for answers. Mr Prime Minister, what do you think happened to MH370? That is next on 60 Minutes.


PART 3

SARAH ABO:
How are you feeling about meeting the Prime Minister?

DANICA WEEKS:
Nervous, so nervous.

SARAH ABO:
Danica Weeks is in Malaysia on an extraordinary mission, and this is D-day.

DANICA WEEKS:
To find our loved ones. And so that's just null and void, as far as I'm concerned.

SARAH ABO:
A scheduled meeting with Prime Minister Mahathir to plead her case to resume the search for MH370.

DANICA WEEKS:
This isn't just about 239 people on a Boeing 777. This is about 8 million people every day that get on a flight. And you know, wives, husbands, family members off for holidays, work, that get on a plane and we don't know what happened.

SARAH ABO:
It's unheard of for a world leader of Dr Mahathir's standing to make time for a personal plea like Danica's. Everyone's tense until Malaysia's 93-year-old strongman makes his entrance.

SARAH ABO:
Good afternoon. Sarah Abo, 60 Minutes. Good afternoon.

DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD:
60 Minutes.

SARAH ABO:
This is Danica Weeks.

DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD:
Nice to leave 15 minutes for me.

SARAH ABO:
Yes, 15 minutes for you.

DANICA WEEKS:
Nice to meet you, sir.

DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD:
Where do I sit?

SARAH ABO:
He is gracious and just a little frail. But this is a man who formerly led his country for nearly 25 years and has now returned to take charge.

DANICA WEEKS:
Thank you, Mr Prime Minister, for taking the time today to come here and speak to me. I'm very grateful.

SARAH ABO:
This is the first time the Prime Minister has met with a relative from MH370.

DANICA WEEKS:
I just wanted to put a personal appeal to you to continue to search for the plane. And in some way, bring all our loved ones home.

DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD:
We intend to continue. And nowadays, with electronic detection, it may be possible for us to find where the plane had come down.

DANICA WEEKS:
Well, that sounds very hopeful, because it is very important, obviously for us, and five years on to have that right and that opportunity to lay my husband to rest and bring him home to us.

DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD:
Yeah, yeah. Not knowing what happened is extremely distressing, because you don't know whether he is somewhere or not. I appreciate that very much.

SPEAKER:
Mr Prime Minister, it seems you do understand the heartache of the families of the victims on board. How would you feel if you had someone on board?

DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD:
God forbid that it should happen to me, but I think I will be very, very upset. Very upset, especially as the search is terminated.

SARAH ABO:
The meeting goes for nearly 30 minutes. The Prime Minister clearly has strong views on the MH370 investigation.

DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD:
Not knowing whether they are alive or dead, not knowing where they may be, I mean, this is extremely upsetting.

SPEAKER:
What do you think happened to MH370?

DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD:
One of the things that I heard from the very beginning was that the plane was hijacked. But a plane of this size going down into the sea anywhere or on land must leave signs. But here, there is absolutely no evidence. It's strange, as if suddenly the plane just vanished.

SARAH ABO:
Being here in Malaysia, it seems there is a sense of national pride in Captain Zaharie's innocence. Is that a blind pride?

DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD:
I cannot think that a person who has been flying for so long, a very senior pilot, would want to do that. I don't know how he can make it disappear. I don't think anybody can answer this question.

ANTHONY LOKE:
We are committed to resume the search if there is a credible evidence, and we
would like to see that we can find the plane and to give closure to the families.

SARAH ABO:
After our meeting with Dr Mahathir, he instructs his Transport Minister Anthony Loke, who has refused all previous interviews about MH370, to talk to us. Is national pride blinding you to the possibility that Captain Zaharie could be responsible?

ANTHONY LOKE:
Well, I mean, until and unless we find the plane and we find the black box, nobody can put any blame to anybody.

SARAH ABO:
But is there a flaw in cancelling him out?

ANTHONY LOKE:
Well, we do not discount anything. I do not think that we discounted any evidence. But I think it's not fair to blame anybody at this point of time.

SARAH ABO:
But when we look at his history, we look at the flight simulator programme of his home, mapping a very similar course into the Southern Indian Ocean?

ANTHONY LOKE:
We have never discounted any possibilities, and we are still committed for the search and to find the plane. So, I mean, as far as we are concerned, our main focus is that we hope that there are more credible evidence that will surface in the months to come so that search can be resumed.

(MUSIC)

SARAH ABO:
Then, by way of helping prove Malaysia's renewed commitment to the investigation, the Minister grants us what has been denied to all other media for years – direct access to the actual wreckage of MH370.

SARAH ABO:
It's eerie to think this fragment represents a giant aircraft lying somewhere at the bottom of an ocean along with its passengers and crew. Fewer than 30 pieces of wreckage which may belong to the plane have ever been found. Only three, including this, have been confirmed as MH370.

(MUSIC)

SARAH ABO:
In the greatest of all aviation mysteries, this is hallowed ground. For international air crash investigators who've never had the chance to examine it, this piece of wreckage is key to finding out what really happened to the aircraft. But our access only emphasises a new commitment to openness we've discovered in Malaysia.

EAN HIGGINS:
I think one thing among others is that, for the first time, a television crew has actually seen the wreckage, seen the flap. Now, it's quite an achievement in its own right. It's quite a scoop, journalistically, but it's more than that, I think. What it shows is that the Malaysians are starting to open up. They are opening up to the West, to Western journalists. It all shows a capacity to look at this again and come to possible conclusions as to what might have happened to the aircraft.

SARAH ABO:
But for that to happen, a decision must be made at the very top, from Dr Mahathir himself.

GRACE NATHAN:
Very much loved, and very much… Many people look up to him. So, whatever he thinks and feels will automatically garner the support of a vast majority of Malaysians.

SARAH ABO:
Grace Nathan is the official spokesperson for the relatives of those lost on MH370. Her mother Anne Daisy was among them. She's astonished at news of Danica's private meeting with Dr Mahathir. How important is it to get Prime Minister Mahathir across the line, if Danica has planted a seed in his mind about finding MH370?

GRACE NATHAN:
I think it's integral. I think it'll be his decision, or his vote of confidence would be what sets everything in motion. Because he's not only the prime minister, but he's a very revered man He has the ultimate say. And if he says it's a go, then we can rest assured that it will happen.

SARAH ABO:
Do you, Mr Prime Minister, pledge to never give up searching for MH370?

DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD:
Losing an aircraft is nothing, but losing people is something else. I mean, you can't sleep thinking about it. What has happened, what has happened? You keep on asking yourself that question, and you get no answer. For as long as there is hope, we will continue to think of ways and means to find out.

SARAH ABO:
Thank you very much for your time, Mr Prime Minister. Really appreciate that. It is clear Dr Mahathir has been touched by Danica's plea.

DANICA WEEKS:
Please don't give up on us. Thank you.

(MUSIC)

SARAH ABO:
For now, it's between a Prime Minister and a mother. And the hope that MH370 isn't lost forever. It is just missing, waiting to be found when the world wills it.

I'm Sarah Abo. It's not just the despairing family and friends of the 239 men, women and children who were on board Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 who deserve answers about what happened to the plane. Everyone who flies needs to know where the Boeing 777 is, and why it ended up there. Big, modern airliners just can't vanish without explanation. In a few days, there'll be another grim MH370 milestone – it'll be five years since the plane went missing. But Danica Weeks, whose husband Paul was a passenger, will never lose hope this mystery will eventually be solved. And to help, she's meeting Malaysia's prime minister, Dr Mahathir Mohamad, to convince him more must be done. (MUSIC) SPEAKER: You have to go through here. And into the middle. DANICA WEEKS: Into the middle. Oh, this is the real maze. Maze of all mazes. They're six and eight. I mean, they were babies. And I just go, "What happened?" It just… It tears at you because you know what Pauly wanted to do with them, and he's not there, and I don't even know where the hell he is. And I just feel so awful. I just want to bring him back. I just want to grab him. (MUSIC) SARAH ABO: MH370. It's the flight number that will haunt public imagination. SPEAKER: The Boeing 777 is missing. Flight MH370 would vanish from radar contact. SARAH ABO: The early hours of March 8, 2014. 239 men, women and children perished. No clue to their fate has ever been found. DANICA WEEKS: Every single plane crash has an answer. MH370, we have nothing. SARAH ABO: But could things be about to change, with Malaysia's strongman prime minister back in charge. Mr Prime Minister, what do you think happened to MH370? Tonight, an unprecedented meeting with Dr Mahathir and, on his order, access to the investigation's secret vault. Is this flap the smoking gun of aviation's greatest mystery? (MUSIC INTENSIFIES) SPEAKER: If you look very carefully, really carefully, you can see it's actually a turn to the left. Then start a long turn to the right and then do another left turn. SARAH ABO: In the five years since MH370 disappeared, 60 Minutes has been chasing the truth. SPEAKER (JOHN): Every day that went by, the mystery grew deeper and this became very quickly unlike any accident in aviation's history. SARAH ABO: With every new breakthrough, suspicion – even certainty to some aviation experts – has closed in on MH370's captain Zaharie Ahmad Shah. SPEAKER: He was killing himself. Unfortunately, he was killing everybody else on board and he did it deliberately. SARAH ABO: But in all that time, those in charge of the Malaysian investigation have never agreed to answer the allegation that the pilot in command committed the worst crime in aviation history. SPEAKER: That's it. SARAH ABO: Until now. (MUSIC) FUAD SHARUJI: I went numb. That is one of the airline's nightmare. It's my nightmare that, to find out that one of our flights have gone missing. SARAH ABO: Crisis manager Fuad Sharuji was in charge of Malaysia Airlines' response on that terrible day five years ago. He's one of the top-level players in the MH370 tragedy who's now speaking for the first time. How many things went wrong that night? FUAD SHARUJI: Everything went wrong. SARAH ABO: In all your decades of experience, has anything like this ever happened before? FUAD SHARUJI: No, never. (MUSIC) FUAD SHARUJI: It was on the early morning of March 8 at 2:30 in the morning when I received the first phone call that we have lost contact with MH370. And I knew that there was something wrong, seriously wrong. So, we immediately activated our code red. I left my house immediately to our emergency operation centre. SARAH ABO: Fuad was not only managing a crisis unlike any in aviation history. For him, it was also personal. The man at the controls of MH370 was a man he knew well - popular Malaysia Airlines pilot Captain Zaharie Ahmad Shah. SARAH ABO: Was there anything peculiar about his final words? FUAD SHARUJI: His final words was, "Goodnight, MH370." RADIO TRANSMISSION: Goodnight, Malaysia 370. FUAD SHARUJI: His voice was calm, relatively calm. There was no signs of anxiety at all. There was nothing abnormal with his last words. EAN HIGGINS: Most people in the professional aviation industry believe that after that transmission, Zaharie hijacked his own aircraft, killed those on board by depressurising it and flew it to its doom in the middle of nowhere in the Southern Indian Ocean. SARAH ABO: For journalist and author Ean Higgins, MH370 has become a professional obsession. What would the world have been thinking when MH370 went missing? EAN HIGGINS: Well, I think the world would have been thinking that this plane must be found and will be found within a few days. Because they are always found, the wreckage, or whatever, or the debris. And people thought, well, one, two, three, four days, we'll have the answer to the mystery. SARAH ABO: In Perth, Danica Weeks and her then infant sons at home were waiting for a call from her husband, Paul, due to land in Beijing on MH370. Two weeks later, Charles Wooley was with her when Malaysia Airlines finally declared there was no hope. SPEAKER: This news was very devastating for the families. DANICA WEEKS: I remember saying then that 18 days was such a long time to wait. 1,800 days has been hell on earth. SARAH ABO: For the last five years, Danica has refused to give up hope of finding an answer for what happened to Paul. Now that hope is taking her to Malaysia. For weeks, on Danica's behalf, 60 Minutes has been in contact with Malaysia's iconic leader, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohammed. And in a move that stunned even his closest advisors, he has agreed for the first time to meet a relative of one of those lost on MH370. Danica will plead her case directly to Dr Mahathir. To reopen the investigation, to renew the search for the flight that took her husband. DANICA WEEKS: We're here for a very good reason, darling. To help find Daddy. SARAH ABO: Do you see this meeting with Dr Mahathir as your last hope? DANICA WEEKS: Yes. This is it. This is my last ditch effort. And as I say, is the pinnacle, it's as high as I can go. It'd just be nice to speak with him and really get him to understand where us, as the families, are coming from. SARAH ABO: How significant is it in your view that Dr Mahathir has agreed to meet with Danica? EAN HIGGINS: I think it's very significant. I think what it shows is that, despite all, he is open to listening to the possibility of re-opening a search. And, of course, if he were to decide on such a course of action, the country, which supports him greatly, would be right behind him. (MUSIC) SARAH ABO: What makes this meeting remarkable is that for years, authorities here have closed ranks against foreigners scrutinising Malaysia's handling of MH370, defending the country's reputation with official silence. But with Dr Mahathir's new government, that silence may be breaking. Coming up, damning evidence. The smoking gun is an eerie course he plotted on a home flight simulator program. Why MH370's captain is to blame. SPEAKER: There is nowhere to land anywhere even close to that part of the world. SARAH ABO: And why Malaysia says he isn't. PETER CHONG: Commit mass murder, no way. SARAH ABO: No possibility? PETER CHONG: No possibility. Certainly not the Captain Zaharie that I know. PART 2 SARAH ABO: Five years on and the theories about what happened to MH370 range from the mystifying to the ridiculous. But the one that most international experts now believe is the only reasonable explanation based on known facts is that MH370 was hijacked by its own pilot, Zaharie Ahmad Shah, who then committed an act of mass murder. But while his name rings in infamy around the world, here in Malaysia, his innocence is an almost sacred truth. EAN HIGGINS: I think it's pretty simple. They don't want to lose face. It's very important in Asian cultures. It's a government owned airline and it's not a good look for Malaysia to have one of its nationals, one of its pilots, take 238 innocent people to their deaths. SARAH ABO: But Malaysia Airlines' crisis manager Fuad Sharuji will always defend his captain. For the record, did Captain Zaharie deliberately crash MH370 into the Southern Indian Ocean and kill everyone on board? FUAD SHARUJI: We don't believe so. For a person to actually take the lives of 239 passengers and crew on board, including his own life, must be a completely deranged person. Madman, crazy. And none of that is the character of Captain Zaharie. PETER CHONG: Anybody that knows Captain would immediately tell you that he's not this kind of person that would do such a thing. SARAH ABO: Peter Chong is another close friend of Zaharie Ahmad Shah. The two were bonded by their passion for politics, which some speculate was the motivation for Captain Zaharie to deliberately crash his plane. So he was very politically active? PETER CHONG: He was very politically concerned. SARAH ABO: Have you allowed yourself to believe that Captain Zaharie did commit mass murder? PETER CHONG: To commit mass murder, no way. SARAH ABO: No possibility? PETER CHONG: No possibility. Certainly not the Captain Zaharie that I know. SARAH ABO: Do you accept that you may not have really known him? I mean, do we really know people? PETER CHONG: Obviously, there is a possibility, but very small percentage. SARAH ABO: Once of the greatest mysteries in the riddle of MH370 is how and where Captain Zaharie spent his final days and hours. Was this a man preparing to commit one aviation's most terrible and heartless crimes? And if so, why? Captain Zaharie's last hours alive could provide the telling clue. SARAH ABO: Those who point to Zaharie's guilt believe he was outraged at the trumped-up conviction of a man he believed was Malaysia's political saviour – Anwar Ibrahim. The conviction was handed down just hours before Captain Zaharie took off in MH370. There's also speculation he left a note behind, never revealed by the authorities. Journalist Ean Higgins. EAN HIGGINS: It was a pretty extraordinary coincidence. But did he leave a message and either it was never found or it got into other hands? Unless there's some part of the puzzle we don't know about, is that there was no claim of responsibility. What's the point of doing something like that, making a political protest, if you don't let anyone know why you're doing it? SARAH ABO: While a motive for Captain Zaharie's involvement is almost impossible to pinpoint, to many, the smoking gun of his guilt is an eerie course he plotted on his home flight simulator program only weeks before he guided MH370 into the night skies of Kuala Lumpur. The course mapped by Captain Zaharie is chillingly close to the presumed actual route of MH370. EAN HIGGINS: It made no sense whatsoever. It went up the Straits of Malacca, as MH370 did, and turned left, south, to the Southern Indian Ocean. There's nowhere to land anywhere even close to that part of the world. It could only have been a suicide flight. SARAH ABO: But despite this damning evidence, senior Malaysian officials still maintain there was nothing suspicious about Captain Zaharie's flight simulation. Even though, for the first time tonight, they admit it did stand out amongst the thousand other flight simulations recovered from his computer. FUAD SHARUJI: It's nothing unusual for pilots to have simulators at home, and to use that for training. SARAH ABO: Why do you think he would've tracked a course deep into the Southern Indian Ocean? FUAD SHARUJI: OK. He also tracked 1,000 other flights. SARAH ABO: Mm-hm. Did any of them end in the middle of nowhere? FUAD SHARUJI: Only one out of the 1,000 flights was in the South Indian Ocean. SARAH ABO: To land nowhere. Does that make sense? FUAD SHARUJI: I do not know. I cannot explain to you why that one particular flight landed in the South Indian Ocean. But if you are trying to lead me that he tried to ditch aircraft, I wouldn't want to buy that. SARAH ABO: Why would you map a route to the middle of nowhere? PETER CHONG: Because it's a difficult route. For training purposes, that would be ideal. SARAH ABO: But I don't understand. It's a difficult route to where? Where is he hoping to land the plane? PETER CHONG: In the water somewhere, maybe. SARAH ABO: He's intending to land the plane in the water? PETER CHONG: No. For training purposes. SARAH ABO: So, is it a coincidence that it did happen? PETER CHONG: Never know. History may tell us. SARAH ABO: Coming up, inside the investigation's secret vault. It is eerie to think this fragment represents a giant aircraft lying somewhere at the bottom of an ocean with its passengers and crew. A desperate plea to Malaysia's leader… DANICA WEEKS: Please don't give up on us. SARAH ABO: ..and fresh hope for answers. Mr Prime Minister, what do you think happened to MH370? That is next on 60 Minutes. PART 3 SARAH ABO: How are you feeling about meeting the Prime Minister? DANICA WEEKS: Nervous, so nervous. SARAH ABO: Danica Weeks is in Malaysia on an extraordinary mission, and this is D-day. DANICA WEEKS: To find our loved ones. And so that's just null and void, as far as I'm concerned. SARAH ABO: A scheduled meeting with Prime Minister Mahathir to plead her case to resume the search for MH370. DANICA WEEKS: This isn't just about 239 people on a Boeing 777. This is about 8 million people every day that get on a flight. And you know, wives, husbands, family members off for holidays, work, that get on a plane and we don't know what happened. SARAH ABO: It's unheard of for a world leader of Dr Mahathir's standing to make time for a personal plea like Danica's. Everyone's tense until Malaysia's 93-year-old strongman makes his entrance. SARAH ABO: Good afternoon. Sarah Abo, 60 Minutes. Good afternoon. DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD: 60 Minutes. SARAH ABO: This is Danica Weeks. DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD: Nice to leave 15 minutes for me. SARAH ABO: Yes, 15 minutes for you. DANICA WEEKS: Nice to meet you, sir. DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD: Where do I sit? SARAH ABO: He is gracious and just a little frail. But this is a man who formerly led his country for nearly 25 years and has now returned to take charge. DANICA WEEKS: Thank you, Mr Prime Minister, for taking the time today to come here and speak to me. I'm very grateful. SARAH ABO: This is the first time the Prime Minister has met with a relative from MH370. DANICA WEEKS: I just wanted to put a personal appeal to you to continue to search for the plane. And in some way, bring all our loved ones home. DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD: We intend to continue. And nowadays, with electronic detection, it may be possible for us to find where the plane had come down. DANICA WEEKS: Well, that sounds very hopeful, because it is very important, obviously for us, and five years on to have that right and that opportunity to lay my husband to rest and bring him home to us. DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD: Yeah, yeah. Not knowing what happened is extremely distressing, because you don't know whether he is somewhere or not. I appreciate that very much. SPEAKER: Mr Prime Minister, it seems you do understand the heartache of the families of the victims on board. How would you feel if you had someone on board? DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD: God forbid that it should happen to me, but I think I will be very, very upset. Very upset, especially as the search is terminated. SARAH ABO: The meeting goes for nearly 30 minutes. The Prime Minister clearly has strong views on the MH370 investigation. DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD: Not knowing whether they are alive or dead, not knowing where they may be, I mean, this is extremely upsetting. SPEAKER: What do you think happened to MH370? DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD: One of the things that I heard from the very beginning was that the plane was hijacked. But a plane of this size going down into the sea anywhere or on land must leave signs. But here, there is absolutely no evidence. It's strange, as if suddenly the plane just vanished. SARAH ABO: Being here in Malaysia, it seems there is a sense of national pride in Captain Zaharie's innocence. Is that a blind pride? DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD: I cannot think that a person who has been flying for so long, a very senior pilot, would want to do that. I don't know how he can make it disappear. I don't think anybody can answer this question. ANTHONY LOKE: We are committed to resume the search if there is a credible evidence, and we would like to see that we can find the plane and to give closure to the families. SARAH ABO: After our meeting with Dr Mahathir, he instructs his Transport Minister Anthony Loke, who has refused all previous interviews about MH370, to talk to us. Is national pride blinding you to the possibility that Captain Zaharie could be responsible? ANTHONY LOKE: Well, I mean, until and unless we find the plane and we find the black box, nobody can put any blame to anybody. SARAH ABO: But is there a flaw in cancelling him out? ANTHONY LOKE: Well, we do not discount anything. I do not think that we discounted any evidence. But I think it's not fair to blame anybody at this point of time. SARAH ABO: But when we look at his history, we look at the flight simulator programme of his home, mapping a very similar course into the Southern Indian Ocean? ANTHONY LOKE: We have never discounted any possibilities, and we are still committed for the search and to find the plane. So, I mean, as far as we are concerned, our main focus is that we hope that there are more credible evidence that will surface in the months to come so that search can be resumed. (MUSIC) SARAH ABO: Then, by way of helping prove Malaysia's renewed commitment to the investigation, the Minister grants us what has been denied to all other media for years – direct access to the actual wreckage of MH370. SARAH ABO: It's eerie to think this fragment represents a giant aircraft lying somewhere at the bottom of an ocean along with its passengers and crew. Fewer than 30 pieces of wreckage which may belong to the plane have ever been found. Only three, including this, have been confirmed as MH370. (MUSIC) SARAH ABO: In the greatest of all aviation mysteries, this is hallowed ground. For international air crash investigators who've never had the chance to examine it, this piece of wreckage is key to finding out what really happened to the aircraft. But our access only emphasises a new commitment to openness we've discovered in Malaysia. EAN HIGGINS: I think one thing among others is that, for the first time, a television crew has actually seen the wreckage, seen the flap. Now, it's quite an achievement in its own right. It's quite a scoop, journalistically, but it's more than that, I think. What it shows is that the Malaysians are starting to open up. They are opening up to the West, to Western journalists. It all shows a capacity to look at this again and come to possible conclusions as to what might have happened to the aircraft. SARAH ABO: But for that to happen, a decision must be made at the very top, from Dr Mahathir himself. GRACE NATHAN: Very much loved, and very much… Many people look up to him. So, whatever he thinks and feels will automatically garner the support of a vast majority of Malaysians. SARAH ABO: Grace Nathan is the official spokesperson for the relatives of those lost on MH370. Her mother Anne Daisy was among them. She's astonished at news of Danica's private meeting with Dr Mahathir. How important is it to get Prime Minister Mahathir across the line, if Danica has planted a seed in his mind about finding MH370? GRACE NATHAN: I think it's integral. I think it'll be his decision, or his vote of confidence would be what sets everything in motion. Because he's not only the prime minister, but he's a very revered man He has the ultimate say. And if he says it's a go, then we can rest assured that it will happen. SARAH ABO: Do you, Mr Prime Minister, pledge to never give up searching for MH370? DR MAHATHIR MOHAMAD: Losing an aircraft is nothing, but losing people is something else. I mean, you can't sleep thinking about it. What has happened, what has happened? You keep on asking yourself that question, and you get no answer. For as long as there is hope, we will continue to think of ways and means to find out. SARAH ABO: Thank you very much for your time, Mr Prime Minister. Really appreciate that. It is clear Dr Mahathir has been touched by Danica's plea. DANICA WEEKS: Please don't give up on us. Thank you. (MUSIC) SARAH ABO: For now, it's between a Prime Minister and a mother. And the hope that MH370 isn't lost forever. It is just missing, waiting to be found when the world wills it.

metadata.Summary: It was a routine scheduled flight from Kuala Lumpur International Airport to Beijing Capital International Airport, carrying 239 passengers and crew – but five years ago Malaysian Airlines flight MH370 disappeared from the radar while flying over the Indian Ocean. An intensive search and investigation followed with some of the world’s top investigators, but with little progress over the years, it remains unclear why the plane went down. Now for the first time investigators have opened up the vault which contains the only recovered parts of the wreckage from the doomed flight.
